title: Binary Number with Alternating Bits
statement: You are given a positive integer `n`. Write `n` in binary without leading zeros and return `true` if every two neighbouring bits are different (the bits go 1, 0, 1, 0, ... from the top), or `false` if some two neighbouring bits are equal. A number with a single bit has no neighbouring pair, so it counts as alternating.
notes:
## Intuition

The direct way is to turn `n` into a binary string and compare neighbouring characters. The same check works on the number itself: `n & 1` reads the lowest bit and `n >> 1` drops it, so walking from the lowest bit upward and comparing each bit with the one before it needs no string at all. The first equal pair settles the answer as `false`; reaching the top bit without one means `true`. (A neat constant-time variant: `n ^ (n >> 1)` is all ones exactly when the bits alternate, and an all-ones value `x` has `x & (x + 1) === 0`.)

## Approach

1. Read the lowest bit into `previous` and shift it off `n`.
2. While `n` still has bits, read its lowest bit into `bit`.
3. If `bit` equals `previous`, two neighbours match: return `false`.
4. Otherwise make `bit` the new `previous` and shift `n` right by one.
5. When no bits remain, every neighbouring pair differed: return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 5` is `101` in binary. `previous = 1` and `n` becomes `10` (2). Next `bit = 0`, which differs from 1, so `previous = 0` and `n` becomes `1`. Next `bit = 1`, which differs from 0, so `previous = 1` and `n` becomes 0. The loop ends and the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log n): one step per bit, at most 31.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Only the bits up to the highest 1 matter; the leading zeros of a 32-bit word are not part of the pattern, which is why the loop stops at `n > 0`.
- `n = 1` has a single bit and must return `true`.
- Use a right shift (`>>`) on non-negative values; in JavaScript, `n / 2` without flooring would produce fractions.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | the bits of the input not yet examined |
| `previous` | the bit just below the current one |
| `bit` | the lowest remaining bit of `n` |

narration.2: Read the lowest bit of n; it is the first bit to compare against.
narration.3: Shift that bit off so n holds the bits still to check.
narration.5: Keep going while n still has a bit set somewhere.
narration.10: This bit becomes the one the next bit is compared with.
narration.13: Every neighbouring pair differed, so the bits alternate.
